A blow on loose ribs is sharper than on a zydeco washboard or scraped board. The player swings the wrist so that the pieces meet by inertia, which gives a triple or a double click, and holding a pair in each hand gives more rhythmic variety. Irish tradition mostly plays one hand, North America often both, which changes the phrasing; the effect is close to the subdivided accompaniment of a banjo roll. The sources give no clear information on range or volume control.

In the United States metal spoons are sometimes used instead. The sources also mention pieces cut flat and straight. The sound source is simply the two pieces of bone, wood or metal striking each other; the instrument is classed as an idiophone, number 111.11, and is found in Europe and North America. 骨頭響板可作為節奏伴奏，出現在愛爾蘭與蘇格蘭傳統音樂、藍調、藍草、齊德科、法裔加: The bones serve as rhythmic accompaniment in Irish and Scottish traditional music, blues, bluegrass, zydeco, French-Canadian music and the Cape Breton music of Nova Scotia. They were also used in nineteenth-century blackface minstrel shows. In the United States a similar technique is often played with spoons instead of bones. In an ensemble they usually provide a fine subdivision of the beat, the wrist driving the pieces together into a continuous, bright pattern.

The player takes a pair of bone pieces, wooden sticks or spoons about 12 to 18 cm long, slightly curved or flat, and holds them between the fingers with the convex sides facing each other. In one method the pieces sit either side of the middle finger, about two thirds of them along the palm and the rest showing past the back of the finger; the hand makes a loose fist, the piece nearer the ring finger is lightly pinned by its tip, and the other hinges between index and middle finger, so that swinging the wrist back and forth makes them strike. The key is not to force them together with the fingers but to let inertia make the stroke; practise the triple click first, then suppress the third with light pressure to get a double click, and once that is fluent combine rhythms, or hold a pair in each hand.

The technique probably reached the United States with Irish and other European immigrants, and the history goes back to ancient China, Egypt, Greece and Rome. In the nineteenth century they appeared in minstrel shows, and they entered Irish and Scottish traditional music, blues, bluegrass, zydeco, French-Canadian music and the Cape Breton music of Nova Scotia. Irish players mostly use one hand and North American players both; players include Brother Bones (1902–1974).
